summary: Jesus teaches in the Nazareth synagogue, but His hometown takes offense at the carpenter they knew, and He does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.
key_insight: Nazareth did not deny Jesus’ wisdom or His miracles; they only asked where they came from, and familiarity made them stumble. Mark says Jesus “marveled because of their unbelief.”
story: Jesus went from there to His own country, the town where He had grown up, and His disciples followed Him. When the Sabbath came, He began to teach in the synagogue. {Mk}

Many who heard Him were astonished. “Where did this Man get these things?” they said. “And what wisdom is this which is given to Him, that such mighty works are performed by His hands! Is this not the carpenter, the Son of Mary, and brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? And are not His sisters here with us?” {Mk} Matthew records the question as “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” {Mt}
So they were offended at Him. Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country, among his own relatives, and in his own house.” {Mk}

He did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief. {Mt} He laid His hands on a few sick people and healed them, and He marveled because of their unbelief. Then He went around the villages in a circuit, teaching. {Mk}
differences: Matthew has the townspeople call Jesus “the carpenter’s son”; Mark has them call Him “the carpenter, the Son of Mary.”
Mark alone mentions the Sabbath, the disciples who came with Him, the few sick people He healed, and that He marveled at their unbelief.
Mark says He “could do no mighty work there” except healing a few; Matthew says He “did not do many mighty works there.”
Jesus’ saying in Mark adds “among his own relatives.” The brothers are listed in a slightly different order.

fit.question: Luke tells of Jesus being rejected in the Nazareth synagogue at the start of His ministry (Luke 4:16–30). Is this the same visit?

points.label: Two visits
points.text: In Luke the people try to throw Jesus off a cliff; here they take offense, but Jesus stays to heal a few and moves on. In Luke’s order, that visit comes before Jesus calls Simon Peter to follow Him (Luke 5:1–11); this one comes much later, with disciples following Him. Edersheim and many others hold that Jesus gave His hometown a second hearing.

points.label: One visit
points.text: McGarvey and others think it is the same visit, and that Luke placed it at the front of his Gospel as a preview of Jesus’ ministry. Both accounts have the hometown’s question about His family and the saying about a prophet in his own country (Luke 4:22, 24).

fit.note: On either reading no account is wrong; Luke promised “an orderly account” (Luke 1:3), and an orderly account need not follow strict date order.
fit.short: Many think Jesus visited Nazareth twice, with different outcomes; others think Luke placed this one visit early as a preview.

scene.label: Nazareth
scene.text: Nazareth was a small, obscure village in the hills of lower Galilee. Everyone knew everyone. Even Nathanael had asked, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46).

scene.label: The carpenter
scene.text: The word means a builder or craftsman who worked mainly in wood and perhaps stone. In the second century, Justin Martyr wrote that Jesus had made plows and yokes. The people of Nazareth had hired Him and watched Him work.

scene.label: “Son of Mary”
scene.text: A man was normally named as his father’s son. Calling Jesus “the Son of Mary” may simply mean Joseph had died, or it may hint at old gossip about His birth.

scene.label: His brothers and sisters
scene.text: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and Judas is probably the Jude who wrote the letter. At this point His brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5). Most Protestants read them as children born to Joseph and Mary after Jesus (Matthew 1:25); Roman Catholic and Orthodox tradition holds they were cousins or Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage.

witnesses.matthew: Places the visit right after his chapter of kingdom parables, so teaching about hearing the word is followed by a town that would not hear it. He ties the scarcity of miracles directly to “their unbelief.”
witnesses.mark: Gives the fuller account: the Sabbath, the disciples present, “the carpenter,” the few who were healed, and Jesus marveling. Mark sets it between Jairus’s house, where faith saw a girl raised, and the sending of the Twelve, who will also meet rejection (6:11).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is fully human, a village carpenter with a mother, brothers and sisters, and He is the One whose wisdom and mighty works no hometown could explain. Unbelief did not drain His power; it shut the door on blessing He was ready to give.
seeing.living: The people of Nazareth thought they already knew all there was to know about Jesus. Anyone who has grown up around Him faces the same danger: a familiarity that no longer expects anything. Ask Him to make you astonished again at who He is.
seeing.ponder: Where has knowing a lot about Jesus kept you from expecting Him to do anything?

preaching.big_idea: Knowing all about Jesus is not the same as believing Him.
outline: A man they thought they knew (3)
preaching.watch_for: Mark sets this rejection right before Jesus sends out the Twelve (6:7–13). Turned away by His own hometown, He multiplies His messengers and warns them that some places will not receive them either (6:11).
